Chapter Six: Crossing Over—The Shock of Freedom and the Weight of the Past.
Imagine stepping across a border and feeling the world change in an instant. For someone escaping North Korea, those first few moments in China or South Korea are a blur—fear, relief, confusion, all tangled together. The air smells different. Every sound is unfamiliar. Suddenly, all the rules that once controlled your every move just… vanish.
But here’s the thing: freedom, for all its promise, is never simple.
Picture a woman who’s risked absolutely everything to reach China. She finds herself surrounded by market stalls overflowing with food. She hesitates—does she even have the right to buy something here? The colors are brighter, the noise is overwhelming, people move with a confidence she’s never seen before. And yet, with every step, there’s a shadow of anxiety. She’s an illegal migrant, always looking over her shoulder, afraid of being found and forced back.
Now, think about arriving in South Korea. The adjustment is even more intense. There’s a young man who was once praised for his loyalty back home. Here, he feels invisible. Neon lights, crowded streets, customs he doesn’t understand—it’s like being dropped into a maze. The language, the money, the expectations—it’s all new. Skills that helped him survive before—being cautious, obedient, staying silent—suddenly don’t help at all. He’s free, but at the same time… completely lost.
Most of us can’t imagine how deeply the past sticks with you. Even in safety, old habits are hard to shake. Many defectors still glance over their shoulders, whisper in public, and hide what they really think. The fear of being watched doesn’t just disappear—it follows them into this new life. Some even wake in the night, heart racing, certain they’ve been discovered.
The past doesn’t let go easily. Memories of hunger, loss, and betrayal show up when you least expect them. Picture a mother, finally reunited with her kids after years apart. Trust doesn’t come easily—not even with those she loves most. She worries all the time—about money, about the future, about the family left behind. The guilt feels heavy, and finding a sense of belonging is harder than she ever imagined.
Yet, despite everything, there are moments that shine. Imagine a former teacher watching her children laugh freely for the very first time. She feels hope rising inside her. She learns to navigate the subway, shops in supermarkets, and starts making her own choices. The process is slow. There are setbacks. But every small victory counts—it’s a step toward a new life.
For many, the hardest part isn’t the journey out, but the journey in—learning to live in a world where freedom is real, but so are loneliness and uncertainty. The past shapes every decision, every relationship, every hope for what’s next. Still, even in the cracks between fear and doubt, new possibilities start to take root.
